notes: West leads the ♥8 against 6NT. There are 6 top tricks outside of diamonds (the ♠A, 2 in hearts, and 3 in clubs). South must hope to play diamonds for 5 tricks and that East was dealt the ♠K along with the heart length that he showed in the bidding.

If East has the ♠K then it should be possible for South to come to a 12th trick through some sort of major suit squeeze. There are 2 losers, however, and no useful way to rectify the count down to the 1 loser that a simple squeeze would require. South's only chance is to play for a 2-loser strip squeeze, but it may be necessary to guess the distribution of East's hand in the end game.

After winning West's heart opening lead, South should focus his attention on the diamond suit. With 3 cards missing it is correct to finesse West for the ♦K. South should be careful to start diamonds by leading the ♦J in case West was dealt all 3 outstanding cards in that suit. On the actual layout the ♦J holds the trick as East follows suit.

South should continue by cashing all of his diamond and club winners, noting East's discards. East discards 3 hearts and the ♠10 on dummy's diamonds and follows suit to 3 rounds of clubs. South should cash the ♥A to confirm the count in that suit and West's discard means that hearts were 6-1 (as East's weak 2♥ opening suggested).

South must now decide which defender was dealt the 13th club. If West has that card then East was dealt 3613 distribution and is down to 2 spades and 1 heart. In this case South must exit in hearts to East who will then be endplayed into leading away from the ♠K.

If East was dealt the outstanding club (and 2614 distribution) then South will be sorry if he exits in hearts to East. East will cash the 13th club to defeat the contract. On this layout South must cash the ♠A to drop East's ♠K instead of exiting in hearts.

The defense has discarded well and South has no way of really knowing which defender was dealt the 13th club. It can, however, be shown that West is more likely than East to hold that card. West is known to have been dealt 1 heart and 2 diamonds for a total of 3 known cards in those suits. East is known to have started with 6 hearts, 1 diamond, and the presumed ♠K for a total of 8 known cards in those suits.

Therefore, West is a favorite to hold the 13th club as there are more "spaces" in his hand for that card. South should exit in hearts at the critical point, hoping that East was dealt 3613 distribution and will be will be endplayed into leading away from the ♠K.

The strip squeeze aspect of this deal took place on the run of the diamonds and clubs. East was eventually forced to discard 3 potential heart winners. It was then safe for South to throw East on lead in hearts without having to worry about him winning any more heart tricks.

Strip squeezes mature with 2 or more losers. These squeezes are very useful when it is impossible for the declarer to rectify the count down to the 1 loser that a simple squeeze requires. In this deal, for example, if South had tried to duck a spade or heart trick early in an attempt to rectify the count, he would have destroyed his threat card in the suit that he played. With only 1 threat suit remaining there would be no squeeze.

The contract looks easy as there appear to be only 2 other possible losers (1 each in hearts and clubs). If the club finesse is wrong and hearts are 4-1, however, South has to be careful in order to maintain trump control.

For example, South lays down the ♥A and ♥K and East discards. South drives out the ♥Q, but West's diamond return forces the South hand in trump. South draws West's last trump and crosses to the dummy in spades. When the club finesse loses to West, he will be free to run the diamond suit.

South can virtually guarantee the contract by surrendering a heart trick on the first round of the suit. West can do no better than to win the ♥Q and lead another diamond. South should take the ruff in dummy and return to the ♣A in order to draw the rest of the trump. South then surrenders a club trick to the defense and is able to ruff West's diamond return and win the rest of the tricks.

South should win West's spade opening lead in dummy to preserve the ♠Q as an entry to the closed hand. The correct play is to continue by leading the ♣10 or ♣9 from the dummy. The defense will win and continue spades to South's ♠Q. South leads a club toward dummy, intending to play the ♣9 if West follows small.

If West plays an honor, South can either duck or win dummy's ♣A. In either case, if East discards, the ♥Q will be an entry to the South hand for another club lead toward the dummy. The recommended line of play allows South to make the contract whenever West has 4 clubs (provided the defense cannot take 3 diamond tricks).

If South continues with a spade to dummy's ♠A and leads a club toward the ♣K, East will take the ♣A and the defense will win 3 spade tricks to defeat the contract. South can guard against this danger and make his contract whenever East was dealt no more than 3 spades (along with the ♣A that is required for South to have a chance).

South should duck a spade at trick 3. The defense can do no better than to put South back in his hand, but a second spade duck will sever the defenders' communications in that suit. Declarer can win any return and play a spade to the ♠A. East can win the ♣A when South leads toward his ♣K, but with the long spade in the West hand, the contract is safe.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 3NT. West's heart opening lead is won by South. Even if the defenders have to take their ♦A on the first or second round, South will have only 8 tricks (2 hearts, 4 diamonds, and 2 clubs). South will still need an extra club trick (presumably by finessing against the ♣Q) for his 9th trick.

South should lead the ♣A or ♣K at trick 2 (in case West has a singleton ♣Q). When both defenders follow small, South should lead either the ♦Q and overtake with dummy's ♦K, or lead the ♦10 or ♦9 and overtake with dummy's ♦J. When this wins, South should finesse against the ♣Q with East (South needs this finesse in any case). West discards a spade revealing that South must finesse again in order to pick up the clubs.

South leads another diamond and West follows small leaving South with a decision as to which diamond should be played from the dummy. The ♦K will be the winning play if West started with 3 or 4 diamonds to the ♦A. It will win the trick and South can repeat the club finesse to come to 9 tricks.

Playing dummy's ♦K on the second round will be fatal if East was dealt a doubleton ♦A. With the diamond suit blocked South will have no hope of coming to 9 tricks. South could have made his contract on this layout by playing a low diamond from dummy on the second round of the suit. The diamond suit is now unblocked and South will emerge with an overtrick (or 2 overtricks if the defenders fail to cash their 2 spade winners now).

It is correct for South to play dummy's ♦K on the second round of the suit. If diamonds are 3-2, the ♦A is more likely to be with the 3-card holding than with the doubleton. The fact that West could still have 4 diamonds to the ♦A further bolsters the argument in favor of playing dummy's ♦K.

It appears that the defense will be able to prevent South from ruffing a heart loser in dummy and that the contract depends on South playing the club suit for no losers. Assuming West was dealt the ♠J, South can guarantee the contract on a dummy reversal without having to guess the clubs. South should take a first round club finesse, not caring if East wins the ♣Q.

East will return a heart and South should win the ♥A. South should cross to the dummy in clubs in order to ruff a diamond in the closed hand. South should then play another club to dummy (it would not help the defense for West to ruff at any point) and ruff another diamond. South should cross a third time in clubs (he must be careful with the club spots to make this possible) and ruff dummy's last diamond to complete the dummy reversal.

If West discards (or follows), he allows South to win his 8th trick. If West overruffs South at any point, South will be able to ruff a heart in the dummy at the end. A dummy reversal is characterized by ruffing tricks in the long trump hand in an effort to establish the short trump hand.

If East has all 4 clubs then South will be able to succeed with a trump coup, provided that he takes the precaution of ruffing a diamond in his hand at once. South crosses to the dummy in clubs and West's discard reveals the 4-0 trump break. South ruffs another diamond in hand and cashes 2 high hearts.

In the above layout South can afford to cash his third heart winner. There are several winning sequences from this point. South can, for example, ruff the ♥2 in dummy and cash dummy's remaining trump. With the lead in dummy at trick 12, East's remaining ♣10 doubleton is picked up through a trump coup.

It would, in fact, be an unnecessary risk for South to cash the third round of hearts. If East was dealt a doubleton heart, he could ruff to defeat the contract. South can guarantee the contract from this point by ruffing both of his remaining hearts in the dummy. South gets back to his hand with a ruff in order to ruff his last heart in the dummy as East is forced to underruff. The lead is in the dummy and East's remaining ♣10 doubleton is caught in a trump coup as before.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 6♦. West's heart opening lead should be ruffed in dummy. If South cashes 2 rounds of dummy's diamonds to probe the distribution of the trump suit, he may not like what he learns. If East discards on the second round of diamonds, the contract will be in serious jeopardy.

If, for example, South plays a spade to the ♠K followed by a spade to dummy's ♠A and a spade to ruff in the closed hand, West might overruff. The fate of the contract will then depend upon the position of the ♣Q. South still has 3 heart losers and he will be able to ruff only 1 of these in the dummy. South will be able to set up a spade trick to discard another heart loser, but South will need the club finesse in order to dispose of his 3rd heart loser.

The are several other feasible lines of play and each of these will lose to various distributions of the East-West cards. South's best line is to lead the ♣J from dummy at trick 2 (or after playing 1 round of trump). This play will establish a third club trick while creating a safe entry to the South hand in the form of the ♣10. In practice the defense is likely to win the ♣Q, but South is in control regardless of what suit is returned.
Suppose East returns a spade, as good as anything. South can win in hand and ruff a heart in the dummy.

2 rounds of trump reveal the dangerous 3-1 break, but South can return to his hand safely with the ♣10 and draw West's last trump with the ♦A. Dummy's remaining clubs will provide discards for South's 2 heart losers and the ♠A is available as a dummy entry to access these winners.

On any normal layout of the cards it cannot help the defense to allow dummy's ♣J to hold the trick. If this happens South can succeed whenever diamonds are no worse than 3-1 and spades no worse than 4-2 (and on some layouts where spades are 5-1). South should start spades immediately, leading low to his ♠K followed by a spade to dummy's ♠A.

When both defenders follow in spades, South is almost home. He should continue with a diamond to the ♦A and a diamond back to dummy, revealing 3 diamonds in the West hand. South should continue with a spade ruff in the closed hand. If West overruffs and continues a heart for dummy to ruff (a club is no better), South can ruff a spade to establish a winner in that suit. Dummy has enough black suit winners (and an entry in clubs) to take care of South's 2 heart losers.

It would not have helped West to refuse to overruff on the third round of spades. If instead West discards, South can simply draw the last trump with dummy's remaining honor and ruff a spade to establish an extra winner in that suit. South can now enter dummy in clubs and lose only 1 club trick at the end.

East has a natural trump trick and South's only hope is that he will have to use this trick in the end game to ruff South's spade loser.

South should cash 2 rounds of diamonds, pitching a spade from dummy on the second round. Next South should ruff a diamond in dummy and cash the ♣A and ♣K so that a club can be ruffed in the closed hand. South should then ruff his last diamond in dummy and, fortunately, East follows. Dummy's last club should be played (it is fine to cash the ♥A first, but if South had led the fourth round of clubs earlier, East could then have defeated the contract by discarding a diamond).

If East were to ruff with his natural trump winner then South would discard his spade loser and win the rest of the tricks. East therefore discards and South is able to score another trick with a small trump. South has won 10 tricks and the ♥A and ♥K will score separately, leaving the defense no choice except to compress their sure trump and spade tricks into a single winner at trick 13.

South thus has 4 likely losers, 2 in hearts as well as the minor suit Aces. It appears that South's extra winner in diamonds is useless as there is no helpful discard to make from the dummy.

With correct technique South can succeed when West was dealt certain distributions. South should win West's trump opening lead in hand and draw a second round of trump to which both defenders follow. South's next move should be to knock out the ♦A. West must win the second round of diamonds and return the suit which South must win in the closed hand.
South must then lead the ♣2, executing a Morton's Fork Coup on West. If West takes his ♣A, North-South will have 2 club winners and dummy's ♣Q can be used to discard a heart from the South hand.

If West ducks his ♣A, dummy's ♣Q will win the trick. South can now cross to his hand in spades and play his last diamond, discarding a club from the dummy. South exits with the ♣K to West's ♣A. West is endplayed. He must either lead a heart away from his ♥A or a club conceding a ruff and discard. In either case South will lose only 1 heart trick.

At this point East is known to have started with 6 diamonds and 4 clubs. East is more likely to have been dealt 2146 distribution than 1246 (because North-South started with more hearts than spades). South should therefore finesse West for the ♥8 (this play would not cost if East was dealt 1246 without the ♥8).

When the ♥7 wins, South should draw West's remaining trump and lead toward the ♦Q. East will win the ♦K, but East must give South the last 3 tricks with the ♠AK and the ♦Q. This type of line is often characterized as a dummy reversal even though both the North and South hands started with the same trump length.

In the actual layout, East will win the ♠A and lead his diamond to place the lead in the dummy. South must lose the lead by playing hearts or clubs in order to later reach his hand with a ruff, but West will win this trick and give East a diamond ruff. Eventually, South will lose a club trick and go down in his contract.

South can avoid this danger by surrendering a heart trick immediately in order to cut the defensive communications in that suit (a scissors coup). If the defense switches to diamonds, South wins in dummy and plays a spade to East. East can do no better than to return a club to place the lead back in dummy, but South can ruff a heart back to his hand and draw East's last trump.

The defense does better to continue hearts (instead of switching to diamonds) after South gives up a heart trick. The contract will fail if South ruffs and drives out the ♠A. East will lead a diamond to lock the lead in dummy as before. South will have to lead clubs, but West will gain the lead and give East a diamond ruff.

South can guard against this danger by discarding his club loser on the second round of hearts. The defense can do no better than to play a club, but South wins in the dummy and plays a spade to East's ♠A. East can switch to his singleton diamond to put the lead back in dummy, but South can get back to his hand by ruffing a club. South can then draw East's last trump and win the rest of the tricks.

notes: West leads the ♦K against 4♠. The contract is in danger because West's 2♥ overcall makes it very likely that the ♥A is sitting over the ♥K. South can almost guarantee the contract by playing along elimination lines as long as he makes the unusual play of allowing West's ♦K to win the first trick.

West switches to clubs (a trump shift is actually best) and dummy wins the ♣A. The ♦A is cashed for a club discard. By trading a diamond loser (which West won) for a club loser (which East would win), South ensures that East is never able to gain the lead in clubs. If East had been able to gain the lead, a heart lead through South's ♥K would lead to the defeat of the contract.

South continues by ruffing a club high in order to start eliminating that suit. South crosses to the dummy by overtaking a middle spade with the ♠K and ruffs another club high. South crosses again in trump in order to lead dummy's last club. If East discards on this trick, South can discard a heart, allowing West to win the trick. West will be endplayed into either leading away from the ♥A or leading a diamond to concede a ruff and discard.

If East follows to the fourth round of clubs, South must ruff high (this line also works if West has club length). South can then cross to the dummy in spades and lead a heart with the intention of playing the ♥10 if East follows small. When East plays the ♥Q or ♥J, South covers with the ♥K and West wins the ♥A. Regardless of how East plays, West will be endplayed into either giving South a heart trick or surrendering a ruff and discard.

notes: West leads the ♠7 against 3NT. There are 8 top tricks (3 spades, given the lead, 3 diamonds, and 2 clubs). The contract will be easy if diamonds are 3-2. South should therefore assume that diamonds are 4-1 and plan the play accordingly.

South should start by winning West's spade opening lead in hand (if South wins it in the dummy he may never get a third spade trick). The resulting blockage in spades creates a communications problem. South must play carefully to resolve this blockage due to the unfavorable lie of the East-West hearts and diamonds.

There is a safety play available that will virtually guarantee the contract. South should duck a diamond in both hands at trick 2 (it is fine to unblock the ♠A first). East will switch to the ♥Q which South must duck. East continues with the ♥J and this time South must cover with the ♥K. West wins the ♥A, but cannot effectively continue hearts from his side of the table.

South can win whatever West returns, unblock the ♠A if necessary, and cross to the closed hand in diamonds. South unblocks his remaining high diamond, cashes the ♠K, and then crosses to the dummy in clubs. South can now cash dummy's remaining diamonds to make his contract.

notes: West leads the ♥5 against 4♠. South wins West's heart opening lead, an obvious singleton, in the closed hand. South lays down a high spade and East's discard reveals 3 natural trump tricks in West's hand. With a sure diamond loser and further problems in the club suit, South has some work to do.

South should concede a diamond trick early in the play. This move clears the way for South to ruff diamonds in the closed hand in preparation for an eventual trump endplay against West. East returns a heart for West to ruff and West switches to a low club. South, who was always playing West for the ♣Q (as he needs the ♣J entry to dummy), can either insert dummy's ♣J or win the ♣K in hand and then finesse the ♣J.

South ruffs a diamond in hand and crosses to the dummy in clubs in order to ruff dummy's last diamond. South cashes the ♣K and he must hope that East discards on this trick. In that case South will be able to ruff his remaining club in the dummy and ruff a heart low at trick 11. West overruffs, but he is endplayed into leading away from his ♠Q at the end.

notes: West leads the ♥Q against 6♣. After winning West's heart opening lead, South can maximize his chances when the diamond finesse is wrong by playing for an elimination.

South should cash his top spades. If either defenders drops the ♠Q or ♠J the contract is guaranteed. South will be able to set up an extra winner in spades to take care of one of his diamond losers (by either a ruffing finesse or a loser-on-loser play depending on which opponent has the outstanding spade honor.)

When both defenders follow small in spades, South should cross in clubs and ruff a spade in the closed hand. South should cash his remaining top heart to eliminate that suit before drawing the rest of the trump, ending in dummy.

Dummy's last spade is led and, if East follows, South guarantees the contract by discarding a diamond from his hand. East, the victim of a loser-on-loser endplay, must lead either a diamond into dummy's ♦AQ or a heart to concede a ruff and discard.

If East discards on the fourth round of spades, South should ruff in hand and lead a diamond toward the dummy. If West follows suit with the lowest outstanding diamond, South can duck in the dummy to endplay East. If West follows suit with a higher diamond, South should win dummy's ♦A and cross to the closed hand in clubs in order to lead another diamond toward dummy.

If West has the ♦K then only 1 diamond trick will be lost and if East wins the ♦Q with the ♦K, South will still have a chance. If East was dealt a doubleton ♦K, he will be forced to concede a ruff and discard.

notes: West leads the ♥8 against 4♠. West's heart opening lead is won by South with the ♥A and the dummy's ♣A and ♣K are cashed for a heart discard. South should plan to go after a diamond ruff in dummy, but if he does so at once the contract will fail in the above layout.

East will win the first round of diamonds and cash a heart trick while West discards a club. East will lead another heart which South must ruff high while West discards his remaining club. South continues with a second diamond to East and must ruff East's heart return high.

South can now ruff a diamond in the dummy and attempt to draw trump. East discards on the second round of spades and South cannot afford to overtake with the ♠A. Dummy will have only clubs remaining and West's remaining trump will be promoted into a winner to defeat the contract.

The solution is for South to ruff a club small in hand after cashing the ♣A and ♣K. This play allows South to win a trick with a small trump before West has a chance to discard his clubs. South exits in diamonds to East who cashes a heart trick and plays a third round which South ruffs high. East wins the second round of diamonds and leads another heart, South ruffing high.
South is now in a position to ruff his diamond loser in dummy. The dummy's 2 remaining high trumps will take care of South's 2 remaining small trumps and the ♠A will be left for the last trick.

notes: West leads the ♦K against 6♠. West's diamond opening lead is won by South's ♦A. On the assumption that West was dealt the ♦Q (for his lead of the ♦K) the contract is assured even if West was dealt 4 hearts to the ♥J.

South should draw trump and test hearts by cashing the ♥A and ♥Q. The contract will be easy unless East discards on this trick. In this case South should continue by running the rest of the spades, discarding clubs (or 1 heart and 1 club) from the dummy.

When South plays a club to dummy's ♣A, West is strip squeezed into coming down to 2 hearts and the singleton ♦Q. South continues by leading dummy's remaining diamond and discarding his club loser as West wins the ♦Q. West is forced to lead away from his ♥J at trick 12, allowing South to win the last 2 tricks.

This basic strip squeeze position matures with 2 (or more) losers. A defender is squeezed into discarding either a winner or a safe exit card so that he can later be forced to lead into a tenace. Often the strip squeeze can come to declarer's rescue when he is unable to safely rectify the count down to the 1 loser that a simple squeeze requires. In this deal, if South had tried to lose an early trick, the defense would have returned a diamond to kill dummy's threat in that suit.

notes: West leads the ♣7 against 3NT. South gratefully wins West's club opening lead in hand (gratefully because a spade lead or a high heart lead and a spade shift defeats the contract) and unblocks his other high club. Both defenders follow to 2 rounds of diamonds.

South still has access to only 8 top tricks (the ♠A, 5 diamonds, and 2 clubs) and the spade position is grim. East is certain to have the ♠K sitting over dummy's ♠Q because if West held the ♠K, along with 7 solid hearts missing only the ♥Q, he would have opened the bidding with 1♥ (or 4♥), not 3♥. The good news about West holding 7 hearts is that if East gains the lead he will not have a heart to lead through South's ♥Q.

South's best chance is to hope that East was dealt the outstanding diamond. South should attempt the gambit of giving East an undeserved diamond trick. South will get at least 2 tricks in return regardless of what East returns. The ♠K is as good as anything, but South can win the ♠A and cash his last 2 diamonds. South then crosses to the ♠Q to enjoy dummy's ♣Q, his 9th trick.

notes: West leads the ♥7 against 4♠. East wins the first trick and plays a second round for South to ruff. With the ♣A as a certain loser, South must hope that spades are 3-2 and he must find some way of avoiding a second loser in clubs.

If South plays on clubs before drawing trump, there is a danger that East will win the ♣A (a card he is marked with on the bidding) and play a third round of hearts. East must have 6 hearts for his bidding and, if he was dealt 3 spades as well, the third round of hearts will promote a second trump trick for the defense.

If instead South draws 2 rounds of trump before playing a club to the ♣Q, East will win the ♣A and draw dummy's last trump. South will be left with an inescapable second loser in clubs. The solution is to win the second round of trump with dummy's ♠K in order to lead dummy's ♣2. East must duck and South's ♣K will win the trick.

With a club trick in the bag, South can get home with a dummy reversal, ruffing dummy's remaining hearts in the South hand. South crosses to the dummy in diamonds and ruffs a heart in the closed hand. If West has the outstanding trump, he is welcome to overruff as South will then be able to ruff his second club loser in the dummy. In the actual layout East has the remaining trump so West will discard when South ruffs a heart.

South tries to cross again in diamonds. If East prevents this by ruffing, South will be able to ruff his second club loser in the dummy. East therefore discards, allowing the dummy to win the second round of diamonds. Dummy's remaining heart is ruffed, completing the dummy reversal. South continues playing diamonds and East is welcome to ruff in whenever he wants. The dummy will have all winners except for the ♣Q. The ♣A will win the third (and last) trick for the defense.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 4♠. West wins the first trick and plays a second round of hearts which is ruffed in the dummy. The ♠A is cashed and East wins the second round of spades while West discards. East plays another heart, forcing South to ruff in hand.

It appears that, for South to have a chance, he needs West to hold the ♣Q and ♣J and for diamonds to be 3-3. South leads a club, West splits his honors, and dummy wins. 4 rounds of diamonds come next. If East ruffs low on the 4th round (ruffing high makes things easy), South can overruff and finesse again in clubs, holding the defense to 1 more trick. On the 4th round of diamonds, however, East will discard his remaining club and be sure to win 2 more trump tricks.

It is impossible for South to make 4♠ against best defense on this club layout. The only club distribution that gives South a chance is ♣QJ doubleton with either defender. South should cash the ♣A and ♣K early hoping the ♣Q and ♣J will fall. When East follows with the ♣Q and ♣J, the diamonds come next. If East ruffs the 4th round, South overruffs and leads a winning club. If instead East discards, South discards his last club and loses only 1 trump trick at the end.

If West was dealt the ♣QJ, South will see these cards fall under the ♣A and ♣K. In this case South must cash a third round of clubs followed by exactly 2 high diamonds. Dummy's winning club can now be played and East is held to a single trump trick as before.

notes: West leads the ♦Q against 4♠. East allows his partner's ♦Q to win the first trick. West switches to a club and East wins the ♣A when an honor is played from dummy. East switches to the ♠8.

The only good news is that clubs appear to be 3-2. If East was dealt 4 clubs, he could have given his partner a club ruff to defeat the contract (the defense would later get a heart trick). South still has a certain club loser and another certain loser in hearts. The only real chance is to play for an elimination or partial elimination with the intention of throwing East on lead in clubs and forcing him to break the heart suit.

If West was dealt 3 spades to the ♠10, it is necessary for South to cover East's ♠8 with the ♠9. West covers with the ♠10 (it would not help him to duck) and dummy wins the trick. South should continue with a spade to his ♠A, noting East's discard, followed by a diamond ruff in dummy in order to eliminate that suit. Dummy's high club should be cashed and East thrown on lead in clubs.

If East returns a diamond, South can discard his heart loser and ruff in dummy. South will be able to return to his hand with a heart ruff and use the ♠6 to draw West's last trump. If South had not covered East's ♠8 with the ♠9 he would still have the ♠9 left at this point and West would have the winning ♠10.

If, after being given the lead in clubs, East returns a heart instead of a diamond, South has to guess whether to play the ♥Q or the ♥10. It is correct to play the ♥10, hoping that East has the ♥J and West has the ♥K. If East was dealt the ♥K and West was dealt the ♥J (making it right for South to play the ♥Q at this point) then West would have ruffed his partner's trick when South exited in clubs. A heart return by West would then defeat the contract.

After winning West's heart opening lead, South should immediately duck a diamond trick to the defense. The defense can do no better than to return a heart to South. The ♣K should come next and, when that holds, South should cash the ♦A. South's careful timing is rewarded when West drops an honor under the ♦A.

South should now lead either the ♣3 to a small club in dummy or the ♣J, overtaking with ♣Q. The defense must duck for there to be a problem. South is now well placed to lead toward the ♦J for his 9th trick. The recommended line will also succeed when diamonds are 3-3.

notes: West leads the ♦8 against 4♠. West's diamond opening lead is covered in dummy and won by East with the ♦A. East returns a diamond and West ruffs. West exits in clubs and South wins.

South should resist the temptation to cash his remaining high club to eliminate that suit and then attempt to endplay West with a singleton ♠A. If West was dealt a doubleton ♠A he would have cashed his ♠A before exiting in clubs. Instead, South should lead a spade to West at once, preserving the ♣K as a hand entry. Again West exits in clubs and South wins in hand.

South's only hope is to squeeze East in hearts and diamonds, but West is marked with the ♥K from the bidding. South can succeed with a transfer squeeze if East was dealt the ♥J. The ♥Q should be led to West's ♥K and dummy's ♥A, establishing East's ♥J as the only card that can beat South's ♥10.

South cashes the rest of the spades, making sure to win the 4th round with the ♠J in the closed hand. East is squeezed in hearts and diamonds on the last round of trump. East will discard the ♥J in the hope that West was dealt the ♥10, but South has that card and will use it, along with dummy's diamond winner, to take the last 2 tricks.

South should allow West's ♣K opening lead to hold the first trick so that East is unable to gain the lead in clubs (heart leads by East through South's ♥K102 would not be welcome). West continues clubs and South wins the ♣A. South should draw trump and ruff dummy's last club to eliminate that suit.

South should continue with 3 rounds of diamonds. If West wins the third round of diamonds, he is endplayed into either leading away from the ♥A or conceding a ruff and discard. If East wins the third round of diamonds, his best defense is to return a heart. South must counter by rising with the ♥K and West must win the ♥A. West is endplayed and must either lead away from the ♥J or lead a club to concede a ruff and discard.

notes: West leads the ♣J against 6♦. South wins West's club opening lead in the closed hand. South has a certain spade loser. If a trump trick must be lost then South's best chance is to score all of the small trumps in his hand with ruffs.

South should lead a heart to the dummy at trick 2 and ruff a heart in the closed hand. South should cross in diamonds and ruff another heart. South should cash his remaining high club before crossing back to the dummy in diamonds. When the ♦Q does not fall (otherwise there is no problem), South should cash dummy's ♣K for a spade discard.

South should take another heart ruff in the closed hand and cash the ♠A, followed by a spade to dummy's ♠K. Finally, South should lead dummy's last club. If East has the ♦Q, the contract is certain as South will score his ♦J en passant. If West has the ♦Q, South must hope that West has to follow suit in clubs as South ruffs. In this layout, West is forced to ruff his partner's spade winner at trick 13.

notes: West leads the ♣J against 6♥. South's only obvious loser is in diamonds, but East has suggested extreme distribution for his 5♣ opening. In the actual layout, West will score a trump trick if South is not careful.

If South makes the natural play of covering West's ♣J opening lead with dummy's ♣Q and ruffing East's ♣K, the contract will fail. Suppose South continues by drawing a round of trump with dummy's ♥Q, revealing the 3-0 trump division when East discards. South then cashes the ♠A and ♠K, but East discards on the second round. South ruffs a spade in dummy and returns to the closed hand in hearts in order to ruff another spade.

South must get back to his hand to draw West's last trump, but if East started with 9 clubs then the defense will build the setting trick through a trump promotion. The best South can do is to lead a diamond, but if East can win, he will return a club to promote West's remaining heart into the setting trick.

The contract cannot be made in this layout once the ♣Q is played from dummy at trick 1. South can (and should) succeed by playing dummy's ♣4 to the first trick. East follows small (if he plays ♣A or ♣K he sets up a ruffing finesse position and South's diamond loser will go away) and South should discard his diamond loser to establish fluid communications back to the South hand with diamond ruffs.

West exits in spades (as good as anything) and South wins to test hearts by playing low to dummy's ♥Q as before. South returns to his hand in spades and ruffs a spade in the dummy. South crosses in hearts and ruffs another spade in dummy to establish the suit. Thanks to South's careful play at trick 1, he is now able to get back to his hand safely by ruffing a diamond small. South can draw West's last trump and enjoy his winning spades.
